x.ASV: A Song of Ascents; of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is For brethren to dwell together in unity!
x.Darby: A Song of degrees. Of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
x.KJV: A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
x.YLT: A Song of the Ascents, by David. Lo, how good and how pleasant The dwelling of brethren--even together!

nt: David is using the word **Behold** to focus the attention of his listeners on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Consider]

The terms **good** and **pleasant** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [truly delightful]

x.ASV: It is like the precious oil upon the head, That ran down upon the beard, Even Aaron’s beard; That came down upon the skirt of his garments;
x.Darby: Like the precious oil upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, upon Aaron's beard, that ran down to the hem of his garments;
x.KJV: It is like the precious ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron’s beard: that went down to the skirts of his garments;
x.YLT: As the good oil on the head, Coming down on the beard, the beard of Aaron, That cometh down on the skirt of his robes,

nt: כַּ⁠שֶּׁ֤מֶן הַ⁠טּ֨וֹב ׀ עַל־הָ⁠רֹ֗אשׁ יֹרֵ֗ד עַֽל־הַ⁠זָּקָ֥ן זְקַֽן־אַהֲרֹ֑ן

David assumes that readers will know that the **good oil** being poured on **the head** and **beard** of Aaron refers to Aaron’s anointing as High Priest which was a solemn and joyful occasion. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [It is as good and pleasant as the anointing oil that is pouring down over Aaron’s head and]

Here, **the mouth of his garments** is a common expression that means the opening or neckline of a garment. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the neckline of his garments]

x.ASV: Like the dew of Hermon, That cometh down upon the mountains of Zion: For there Jehovah commanded the blessing, Even life for evermore.
x.Darby: As the dew of Hermon that descendeth on the mountains of Zion; for there hath Jehovah commanded the blessing, life for evermore.
x.KJV: As the dew of Hermon, and as the dew that descended upon the mountains of Zion: for there the Lord commanded the blessing, even life for evermore.
x.YLT: As dew of Hermon--That cometh down on hills of Zion, For there Jehovah commanded the blessing--Life unto the age!

nt: Here the word **there** refers to Zion. David is using this word to refer back to the mountains of Zion that he mentioned previously. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [it was there on Zion that]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the dew of Hermon** is refreshing and life-giving as it falls on the land, so the unity of God’s people is refreshing and brings life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as the refreshing dew from Hermon falls on the mountains of Zion, so the unity of God’s people refreshes and gives life]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the blessing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he would bless his people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **life**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that they would live forever]
